claims.claim: Cartesian doubt became the invisible axis and self-evident motor moving all modern thought, replacing the ancient Greek wonder (thaumazein).
qualifications: applies specifically to modern philosophy and thought since Descartes
claims.supporting_excerpt: Descartes was the first to conceptualize this modern doubting, which after him became the self-evident, in audible motor which has moved all thought, the invisible axis around which all thinking has been centered.

claims.claim: Cartesian doubt ultimately arose from the loss of self-evidence and the insight that neither truth nor reality can be taken on faith or assumed to reveal itself automatically.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This doubt resides ultimately in the loss of self-evidence, and all thought had always started from what is evident in and by itself—evident not only for the thinker but for everybody.

definitions.definition: A radical and universal doubt that occupies a central position in modern philosophy, originating as a response to the new reality where Being and Appearance part company.

distinctions.distinction: Thaumazein was the wonder at everything that is as it is, which served as the center for classical conceptual philosophy from Plato and Aristotle onward, whereas modern philosophy since Descartes has consisted in the articulations and ramifications of doubting.

must_not_be_lost: The characterization of Cartesian doubt as universal and distinct from mere methodological skepticism or sensory deception checks.
The link between the telescope, homo faber, and the parting of Being and Appearance.
output.segment_function: Examines the historical origin and radical, universal significance of Cartesian doubt as the foundational motor of modern philosophy, contrasting it with ancient wonder and traditional trust in sensory and rational evidence.
unresolved_context: Footnotes and external historical references such as Galileo, Aristarchus, Copernicus, Marx, Democritus, and Kierkegaard mentioned in the text.
